cards.note: This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy. It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.
The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen to the south or east from the plains around Naples.
"Corte" means "courtyard". It generally refers to isolated farmhouses or smaller villages. It is most frequent in the area marked although it can appear elsewhere

The Adige Valley is a unique area within the Alps, located within Trentino province. Here you’ll find huge amounts of fruit trees (mostly just apple trees but occasionally vineyards too) against an alpine backdrop, making this region very recognisable.

The Aeolian islands are a volcanic archipelago north of Sicily. Here you will find a mix of volcanic soil and rocks with mediterranean vegetation, like stone pines or olive trees. Like in Sicily, cacti are fairly common.

In the mountains of the islands it is very common to see touristic white villas.

Almond trees are of some use, mostly they blend with areas of heavy olive production, however combinations of almond and olive plantations can be indicative of Northern Puglia rather than the peninsula. Almond trees look similar to olive trees but have more saturated leaves and bloom during the spring.
Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.
The alpine region in northern Italy has tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.

The Amalfi Coast is a distinctive, south-facing stretch of coastline on the Sorrento Peninsula, west of Salerno. Known for its steep cliffs and photogenic views, a dramatic, cliffy coastline almost always means you’re looking at Amalfi.
In Aosta and valleys south of it, you’ll find roofs made of large, diamond-shaped slabs of slate.

Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

NOTE: This can look superficially similar to Andorran architecture.
Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors. The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.
Plain yellow stickers are commonly found on signbacks in this general region:

The Barolo wine region is extremely recognisable as virtually every inch of space is covered by neatly organised vineyards. Once you see it you’ll always be able to recognise it. If you find yourself in such a region I recommend hedging near the city of Alba as Barolo itself is a small village on the edge of this region.

The city of Bologna is famous for its porticoes - covered walkways in place of pavements. These can also be found in most city centres in the area around Bologna, including in nearby cities like Modena and Ferrara, as well as smaller towns.

Cacti in Italy are most common in the south, particularly in Sicily, southern Sardinia and the south of Apulia.

NOTE: They can be found else where + on some of the small islands

The Campione d'Italia exclave in Switzerland can be recognized by its low camera, having a long antenna and a flag. There is also a body of water to the west.

NOTE: This antenna can also be found in several areas in Switzerland.

In the region around the city of Udine the word "Casali" can be found. It basically means "Farmhouses", it often refers to larger farmhouses or is used in streetnames

NOTE: It can appear out of the marked area.

"Cascina" means something like "farmhouse" can be used on top of a road sign, this is a very good indicator for western po valley. It also can be used for village names. NOTE: The word cascina can appear elsewhere.

The Apennines run through central Italy, with the highest peaks in the middle, mostly treeless and snow-free. Key parks include Monti Sibillini and Maiella. Roads cross the highlands mainly near Gran Sasso.
Cherry trees in Italy are heavily concentrated around the town of Vignola near Modena. These are very recognisable for their concrete supports if not the droopy-leafed trees themselves.
Citrus plantations are primarily found on eastern Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria.

Centro Valle Intelvi is a municipalty in the province of Como, located above the city of "Como", on the border to Switzerland. There are 5 villages using the "Intelvi" in their names. Location on the map
The Alps can be tricky to place, but very jagged peaks usually mean you're in the eastern Italian Alps, especially the Dolomites area. (The Dolomites are a part, not the whole range.)
The Dolomiti Lucane has very unique mountains and rock formations confined to a small area in the southern region of Basilicata.

The upper Adige Valley near the tripoint with Switzerland and Austria (as well as connected valleys) is the driest part of the Alps. Here you’ll find very short grass and few trees outside of the mountain slopes.
On the island of Elba, poles are uniquely painted a pale yellow colour.
Etna, the tallest volcano in Europe, can be seen rising above the landscape from far away in eastern Sicily.

The Euganei Hills are a very good reference point within the flat north, marked clearly on Google Maps just southwest of Padua. The hills are very unique and conical, and can often be seen from quite a distance.

In much of eastern Basilicata you can find these interesting exposed limestone formations which are highly distinct and localised. (This can be found in the hills of Emilia-Romagna too but in a far more green landscape).

Apart from the Northern Plain, the only other large flat farming area is near Foggia. It is drier, with more fallow land and olive groves. The surrounding hills are low, bare, and often have wind turbines.
French can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.
The region of South Tyrol has a German majority, and as such uses German bilingual signs.

Around Albenga (Liguria) you will find a huge number of glass greenhouses that look very distinct from the plastic ones in other parts of Italy. You can also find these in smaller numbers in some of the valleys further west towards the French border.
The Gubbio plain in Umbria is one of numerous NW-SE-facing ‘sister’ valleys of the Florence one, and it’s particularly recognisable for the ‘bald’ mountain on the northeast side of it.

Italy is the second-largest hazelnut producer after Turkey, with most grown in Lazio and Campania along the central west coast. A hotspot lies just southeast of Viterbo. Hazelnut trees are easy to recognize by their multiple stems growing from a single base.

While olive trees can be found in most of Southern and even Central Italy, in Calabria olive plantations look quite distinct, with these orderly hillside plantations that are often visible from a distance.
Lomellina is a historical area above Alessandria. There are 10 Towns/villages using "Lomello/Lomellina in their names. Locations on the map.
Polesine is a historical area southwest of Venice. There are 12 Towns/villages using "Polesine" in their names. Locations on the map
Brianza is a historical region above Milan. There are 12 Towns/villages using "Brianza" in their names. Locations on the map
Cadore historical region in the region Veneto near the Austrian border. There are 22 villages using "Cadore" in their names. Locations on the map.
Canavese is a historical region above Turin. There are 24 Towns/villages using "Canavese" in their names. Locations on the map

The island of Favignana has a distinct topography, with mountains running north to south splitting the island in two.

On both sides of the island you will find flat areas, with many rock walls similar to those found in Bari.

Unlike the other islands near Sicily, Favignana is not volcanic.

The island of Pantelleria is a volcanic island southwest of Sicily. Dark volcanic rocks can be seen in the many rock walls of the island, as well as on some houses. It is fairly common to see yellow lichen covering the rocks. The island also has a very large amount of cacti.

The small island of Ponza south of Rome has very unique architecture. Almost all the buildings are boxy with defined outlines along all the edges. Some buildings are also baby blue which is even more unique.
"Lario" is the actual name of Lake Como and some Towns/villages around it use it in their names. Locations on the map.
Liguiria has a very recognizeable architectural style consisting of larger, more elegant, richly coloured houses, often with painted details.

The coastal plain south of Rome is very flat and surprisingly warm given how far north it is. A deadflat area with lots of palms, reeds, stone pines, eucalyptus rows and mountains northeast is a guaranteed Litoral Romano.
Around the mountain Grappa (above Venice) some Towns/villages use "Grappa" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can be seen on other signs in this area not just townsigns.
Around the Cilento Nationalpark (under napels) on the Cilento coast some Towns/villages use "Cilento" in their names. Locations on the map

Around the Nationalpark Gargano (above Bari) some Towns/villages use "Gargano/Garganico" in their names. Locations on the map. Also you can recognize the park itself by the dense forests of lichen and vine covered trees and the abundance of Aleppo pines.

The landscape on the southeastern peninsula surrounding Bari has many olive plantations, which are often seen together with bright rock walls. The dirt in the region typically has a noticeably red colour.

Beware that a similar landscape can also be found in southeastern Sicily.

NOTE: Olive trees are common everywhere in Italy.
In the Ossola Valley, you will find these very unique rocky-looking roofs with small, uneven tiles.

The Padan Plain (commonly referred to as Po Valley) can typically be recognized by its complete flatness. The plain has some of the worst air quality in Europe, which has led to much of the coverage having a noticeable haze.
Plana del Fùcino is a small plain surrounded by mountains in the middle of Italy with a grid of roads going completely north-to-south.

This valley is covered in industrial estates and even more uniquely, vast areas dedicated to growing/storing ornamental plants, something very distinct and unique to this area + Prato is the most Chinese city in Europe and many of the industrial estates around it have Chinese signage.
Monferrato is a region to the east of Turin. There are 24 Towns/villages using "Monferrato" in their names. Locations on the map

Salento is a geographic region at the southern end of the region of Apulia. Towns/villages in this region sometimes use "Salentino" in their names, which is a good clue for the "heel" of the "Italian boto". Locations on the map.
Around the Regionalpark Matese (above Napels) some Towns/villages use "Matese" in their names. Locations on the map.
Rice is mainly produced in the western and central parts of Po valley, and less commonly in Sardinia.

The "Adda" is a river in northern Italy that originates from "Lago di Como" and eventually flows into the "Po River". Towns/villages bordering this river often use the word "abba" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can also be seen on other signs in this region

"Adige" is a river in northern Italy that goes from the Alps, through Bozen, Trento and Verona and eventually ends in the Adriatic sea to the south of Venice. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "all´/sull´/d´Adige" in their names. Locations on the map. Also you can find it on other signs in this region. NOTE: The shortcut a/A for all´Adige can be used.

Brenta is a river originating from "Lago di Caldonazzo" it flows through "Bassano del grappa" all the way down to the south of Venice. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "in/sul/di Brenta" in their names. Also you can find it on other signs in this region. Locations on the map

"Livenza" is a river in northern Italy, its source is near Caneva in the province of Pordenone. It flows in direction of Adriatic Sea and eventually enters it near Caorle. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "(di) Livenza" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can also be on other signs in this region

"Oglio" is a river in north Italy. After flowing through "Lago d´Iseo" it flows southwestward until it enters Po River. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "sull´/d´Oglio" in their names. Locations on the map

"Piave" is a river in north Italy. Its source is in the northwest of the Friuli Venezia Giulia region near the border to Austria. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Piave" in their names. Locations on the map

"Scrivia" is a river in northern Italy, its source is the Po River and it flows till Scoffera (near Genoa). Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Scrivia" in their names. Locations on the map

"Sesia" is a river in northern Italy, its sources are the glaciers of Monte Rosa at the border with Switzerland. It flows through the Alpine valley Valsesia. The Sesia flows into the Po River near Casale Monferrato. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Sesia" in their names. Locations on the map

"Tagliamento" is a river in northern Italy, its source is near Forni di Spora. It flows into the Adriatic Sea southwest from Udine. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Tagliamento" in their names. Locations on the map

"Ticino" is a river in northern Italy. After it flows through Lago Maggiore it flows southeastward till it enters Po River. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Ticino" in their names. Locations on the map
Within the Aeolian islands, Salina can easily be distinguished from the twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.
Cork oak is a good indicator for Sardinia. The tree itself is recognisable when the cork (the bark of the tree) has been harvested, baring its distinctive red trunk.
Eucalyptus is a very good clue for Sardinia, where it is far more common than anywhere else in Italy.

Grey rocks sticking up from the ground are commonly found on Sardinia, particularly in the northeast.

NOTE: A similar phenomenon can be seen on Sicily, however the landscape will typically be much drier than Sardinia and it can be seen elsewhere too.
Italy has a couple ‘seas of plastic’ (similar to the one in southern Spain). Most of these are along the southern coast of Sicily, roughly in these highlighted areas:
Sheep = Sardinia (if not then most likely Tuscany)
The western Sicilian landscape is characterised by an arid, hilly agricultural landscape, often combined with rocky mountains.
Close to the Slovenian border you can find Slovene bilingual signs. NOTE: In this area there are also only italian signs.
Sunflowers are generally found in a belt stretching from Tuscany to Marche, towards the top of the Italian peninsula, although they are a little more common to the eastern end of that belt.
In Northwestern Sardinia you can find many flat-topped mountains with a slight ‘wild west’ feel.
In Friuli and eastern Veneto, you will find many ‘pollarded’ trees lining the roads. This means trees that have been ornamentally trimmed (similar to ‘Colombian trees’).
The Tuscan landscape is very iconic, consisting of rolling hills with loads of cypress trees. You will also commonly find vineyards, stone pines, and sometimes sunflowers and olives here.

A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

NOTE: A similar style of architecture can be found in northeastern Spain.
Arbia is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs
Chianti is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs
Orcia is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

Valdarno is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs
North of Verano you can find the Valpolicella wine region (appears in a few municipality names too), which has these quite distinct terraced vineyards.
Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.
Vineyards in a dead-flat region resembling the Po Valley means you are most likely in Veneto/Friuli towards the eastern end of the great North Italian Plain.
Venice can typically be recognized by its many canals running through most of the city.

Vulcano is perhaps the most easily recognizable of the Aeolian islands, with its volcano having an almost white stripe of dirt following the top of the mountainside. It can typically be spotted from afar on the island.
